Jean-Pierre Melville. A French director who prefigured the New Wave through his cooler, more economical style—spare dialogue, long silences, and a visual aesthetic influenced by American film noir. His crime thrillers and Resistance dramas influenced Godard and Truffaut while remaining distinct from their avant-garde concerns, grounded in genre pleasures and the romance of the outlaw.

He pioneered an independent, studio-free mode of filmmaking in the nineteen-fifties, presaging the New Wave's low-budget autonomy. He directed Le Samouraï in 1967, a glacial crime thriller starring Alain Delon as a perfectionist hitman—an exercise in cool style and silence that became an international cult icon. He made Bob le Flambeur in 1956, a heist film with American noir DNA but French sensibility that influenced countless crime directors who followed.

Melville is known for subdued performances, minimal dialogue, and attention to clothing and gesture over psychological exposition. He was fascinated by ritual and codes of honour—thieves, soldiers, assassins—as structures that replace conventional morality. He composed many scenes with non-diegetic voice-over, a technique he inherited from American noir and deployed with Gallic restraint. He remained a singular figure, neither New Wave nor classical. Younger directors including Godard and Truffaut cited him as a precursor.

Jean-Luc Godard was influenced by Melville's formal restraint and elliptical narrative. François Truffaut admired Melville's genre mastery within a personal vision. Melville channelled the American film noir tradition into French cinema. Alain Delon was his frequent collaborator and the embodiment of Melville's ideal of the laconic protagonist.
